Transduction is how the nervous system converts physical and chemical signals into neural impulses — the process that makes the world around you perceivable. It is the fundamental step of translating a stimulus into an electrical signal. In sensory transduction, specialized sensory receptors take physical or chemical inputs and turn them into precise electrical impulses that travel to the brain.

The visual system is a good example. In the retina, rod and cone cells form the bridge between the physical environment and neural communication. When light strikes these photoreceptors, the protein rhodopsin changes shape. That molecular shift sets off a cascade of events that alters the photoreceptor's electrochemical gradient. As the gradient decreases, so do the electrical signals sent to the brain. In other words, more light hitting the photoreceptor produces fewer electrical impulses — a counterintuitive but remarkably precise mechanism that lets your brain decode the visual world.

Mobile internet is expanding what storytelling can do, bringing electronic games to portable, location-aware interfaces. This is the latest step in a decades-long evolution of electronic games that aim to empower the player—not just as an avatar inside a gameworld, but as a co-author working alongside the original designers.

Location-aware interfaces let players fold real-world places into their gameworld, and vice versa—something no interactive medium has done before. Beyond empowering the player in worldmaking, mobile games abandon linear narratives in favor of cooperative storytelling built on the player's experience of place.

The "author-player" worldmaking concept isn't new, but mobile games push the process past the constraints of traditional video games. By extending worldmaking beyond the screen and into the physical world, location-aware interfaces turn the player's sensory experience of real places into storytelling tools.

Subject: Hitchhiking in the Ruhr Area, Germany — What You Should Know

Dear Customer,

The Ruhr Area (German: Ruhrgebiet), often just called the Ruhr, is an urban region in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. It's made up of many former industrial cities, including Duisburg, Oberhausen, Bottrop, Mülheim an der Ruhr, Essen, Gelsenkirchen, Bochum, Herne, Hamm, Hagen, Dortmund, Recklinghausen, Unna, and Witten.

Around five million people live here — considerably more than in Berlin, Hamburg, or Munich. The region has plenty of motorways, but hitchhiking can still be difficult because the network of minor roads is so complex. The main motorways are the A1, A2, and A3.

If you're planning to hitch here, stick to these major motorways. The smaller roads are nearly impossible to work with, since hardly any transit traffic uses them. Germany is generally a good country for hitchhiking, but the Ruhr Area is by far its least pleasant region for it. Hitching within the Ruhr is a bit like hitching in a huge city such as Istanbul: each city is technically independent, but to a traveler they all blur into districts of one enormous city.
